messages:
Amara Diallo: quick RBAC v2 q for folks thinking about enforcement boundaries. Where do we want permission checks to live long-term—API gateway vs within each service? gateway would be nice for consistency but worried about perf + internal calls bypassing it.

Jordan Lee: we should treat service-level checks as the source of truth. gateway checks can be additive (early reject / nicer error shaping) but not sufficient.
- internal service->service calls + async jobs won’t go through gateway
- defense in depth: even if gateway misconfig/bug, services still enforce
- policy semantics easier to reason about when evaluation happens at the resource owner

Kaitlyn Nguyen: +1. the control plane PR (18432) puts authz middleware in the service so handlers declare `resource/action/scope` and it’s enforced there.
Gateway can still do:
- authn (session/JWT verification)
- rate limiting/quotas
- maybe coarse “is member of org/project” (cheap) before forwarding
But not the fine-grained RBAC v2 decision.

Ethan Park: agreeing in principle, but we need a crisp standard so we don’t end up duplicating checks everywhere w/ different behavior.
Also perf: some endpoints are hot-ish (console polling, list endpoints). If each service does policy eval per request, what’s the target budget?

Jordan Lee: perf budget proposal: p95 authz evaluation < 1ms (excluding network) and mostly cache hits.
Strategy:
- cache policy bundle + derived role->permissions per org (or per policy_version)
- cache role assignments per user/org (short TTL + invalidation on writes)
- evaluation is basically set membership + scope matching
Worst-case should degrade gracefully: allow request to proceed to service w/ “unknown” shouldn’t happen; but if cache miss -> fetch policy once per org and reuse.

Benji Okafor: what about calls between control plane services? e.g. billing service calling org service. those won’t have an end-user actor.

Kaitlyn Nguyen: we need actor types in the authz context.
I’m assuming:
- end_user (from session/JWT)
- service_principal (for internal calls)
- support / break-glass (separate path)
Internal calls should use service principals that map to a constrained role (or explicit allowlist). We should NOT “skip authz for internal traffic” by default.

Brian Murphy: standard should be: “every externally reachable endpoint MUST declare a permission + enforce in service”.
Gateway can optionally pre-check but can’t be the only enforcement.
Also we need consistent error behavior:
- HTTP 403
- structured reason code (e.g. `AUTHZ_DENY_MISSING_PERMISSION`, `AUTHZ_DENY_SCOPE_MISMATCH`)
- don’t leak sensitive policy details in the message

Allison Grant: and logging/tracing consistency:
- always log allow/deny with `actor_id`, `actor_type`, `org_id`, `project_id` (if any), `resource`, `action`, `scope`, `policy_version`, `role_ids`
- for denied requests, add `decision_reason` and emit metric
We’ll want this for audit log enrichment + debugging shadow-denies.

Ethan Park: one more nuance: if gateway does pre-checks we need to be careful about double-eval divergence (policy cache mismatch etc). don’t want gateway denying while service allows.

Jordan Lee: yep. if we do gateway checks, they should be “fail open” during rollout (log-only) OR strictly use the same library + same cached policy source.
But IMO keep it simple: gateway does authn + forwarding, services do authz.
Once we’re stable we can add optional gateway “fast deny” for obviously forbidden actions.

Kaitlyn Nguyen: implementation-wise we’re planning a shared authz lib so gateway/service can literally call the same evaluator if/when we choose.
Perf numbers from local bench (rough):
- cache hit eval: ~80–150µs
- cache miss pulling policy from in-memory store: ~1–2ms (first time per org)
Need to test in staging with realistic org sizes.

Benji Okafor: what about the console backend vs control plane? console backend is a separate service. do we enforce there too?

Brian Murphy: yes. console backend endpoints are externally reachable. they should enforce, even if they’re just proxying to control plane.
If console backend is proxying, it still needs to protect “console-only” routes (e.g. admin UI actions) and ensure it’s not trusting upstream too much.

Allison Grant: and for proxy calls, propagate authz context (actor + org + request id) for audit correlation. Otherwise we end up w/ “unknown actor” events in downstream.

Amara Diallo: ok, so the guidance is:
1) service-level checks are mandatory
2) gateway checks optional + must share lib/policy source + avoid deny divergence
3) perf budget ~<1ms p95 w/ caching
4) consistent 403 reason codes + structured logs
I’ll document this in the eng standard and align with Kaitlyn on whether gateway does anything beyond authn/rate-limit for phase 1.

Ethan Park: sounds good. can we add a CI guardrail too? like endpoints must declare permission annotation.

Kaitlyn Nguyen: already on the roadmap (conformance tests). we can make it fail builds if a new route lacks permission declaration.

Jordan Lee: :thumbsup: I’ll also add a note to ADR thread: “enforcement in resource-owning service; gateway optional.”

Amara Diallo: thanks all. I’ll sync with Connor on rollout so we don’t accidentally add gateway denies during shadow mode.
